title: 3rd Sitting of third session of 2025
summary: The 3rd sitting of the third session of 2025 opened at 09:02 on 7 October 2025. After three written ministerial answers on a planned national drug-prevalence survey, two bills were introduced for first reading and a constitutional amendment bill on ministers' asset disclosure had its opening debate closed with no one else speaking. Members then debated the government's re-employment bill, which would let people stay in or return to work past the current retirement age of 65, up to 75; almost every speaker backed it, with some asking for safeguards for younger workers and for people who retired earlier. After a break from 10:31 to 11:01, debate began on a resolution urging faster investigation of corruption flagged in the Auditor General's special audit of Fenaka Corporation, and it was still under way when this part ends. The text has dropped marks and jumbled digits, so the attendance figures are read as printed. This part opens in the middle of a debate about corruption raised by the Fenaka audit report, with the Central Hithadhoo and Addu Meedhoo members speaking. Members then debated a bill to amend the 2009 land transport law (Law No. 2009/5), with the South Fuvahmulah and Mathiveri members speaking before the sponsor, the North Galolhu member, had the final word. After a recess the chair put three bills to a vote on whether the House accepts them for study: a constitutional amendment bill and a land transport bill from the North Galolhu member, and a government employment bill. All three were accepted and sent to committees, and the next sitting was set for 8 October 2025. The text is garbled in places.

speakers.name: Mohamed Ibrahim
positions: Asked in three written questions how far the drug prevalence survey and Drugs Act amendment had got and what is known about drug use in Male'.
Presented his bill to amend the Constitution so Cabinet members must disclose assets and business interests to the Auditor General within a set time.
Closed debate on his land transport bill, citing growth in motorcycles, cars and traffic accidents and deaths since 2010.
Said widening roads will not fix the problem, and that rules and laws on vehicle numbers need amending.

speakers.name: Dr. Ahmed Shamheed
positions: Did not oppose the re-employment bill but warned it could delay promotions for younger staff and raise recurrent wage costs.
On the Fenaka audit resolution, said earlier special audits had similar findings and urged action on all of them and on officials responsible.

speakers.name: Hussain Hameed
positions: Backed the bill, saying forced retirement at 65 hurts people's mental health, and called for incentives to raise the falling birth rate.
On the Fenaka audit resolution, argued that cash payments make corruption easier and called for a move to a cashless economy and laws to recover stolen money.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Hussain
positions: Backed the bill, citing doctors and other professionals who are forced out at 65 while still skilled.
Said Malé's vehicle congestion and parking shortage need a lasting fix, and that new buildings should be required to provide parking.
Suggested registering electric and battery vehicles in place of petrol ones, noting thousands of motorcycles are imported each year.
Questioned the transport minister's role and urged better ways to register cars brought to Malé from other islands.

speakers.name: Ahmed Naseer
positions: Backed the re-employment bill, saying many retirees are skilled and able, and that young graduates also need jobs.
Backed the Fenaka audit resolution, called for firm punishment for corruption and for regular audits of state companies.

speakers.name: Dr. Anara Naeem
positions: Backed the re-employment bill as a way to give people past 65 more work opportunities as the population ages.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Didi
positions: Backed the bill, saying many trained public servants retire while still able to work and the bill answers that.

speakers.name: Mauroof Zakir
positions: Backed the bill, saying it should not favour any political group, and suggested a probation period for newly re-employed people.

speakers.name: Mohamed Shahid
positions: Backed the bill as a presidential pledge and said the current pension of about MVR 5,000 is too low to live on.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Shujau
positions: Backed the bill, saying people over 65 who want to keep working should be able to, and criticised the previous government's foreign-worker policy.

speakers.name: Ahmed Xamyr
positions: Backed the bill, saying long-serving older staff are left idle at home and the bill helps them stay active.

speakers.name: Ali Moosa
positions: Backed the bill, citing shortages of teachers and medical staff, and asked the committee to refine it.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Falah
positions: Backed the bill as a 2023 presidential pledge and noted that some MDP members also supported it.

speakers.name: Saudulla Hilmy
positions: Backed the bill but raised that only people who left work in the last seven years qualify and asked the committee to look at earlier retirees.

speakers.name: Mohamed Fazeel
positions: Backed the bill, said pensions are very low, and raised unemployed young people such as trained pilots.

speakers.name: Hussain Ziyad
positions: Called the Fenaka audit resolution reasonable but said audits come too slowly and earlier cases went without action.

speakers.name: Abdulla Shareef
positions: Backed the Fenaka audit resolution, citing cable purchases and unfinished buildings in the audit, and urged investigation of those responsible.

speakers.name: Ahmed Azaan Marzooq
positions: Said Fenaka audit findings are not new, that past governments allowed such practices, and that action should start with those who permitted them.
Argued corruption is a systemic problem needing stronger laws, enforcement and political will, citing Singapore as an example.
Said the current government is taking steps against corruption, such as changing heads of some state companies.

speakers.name: Abdul Rahman
positions: Said corruption talk has become a trend, naming the Fenaka and MMPRC cases and saying participants are in both governments.
Described what he saw when he visited Fenaka after the report, and said state funds and equipment such as generators were being wasted.
Said corruption starts at party grassroots level and called on the present government to share responsibility.

speakers.name: Hassan Zareer
positions: Said the bill has good amendments but some need changing.
Argued Malé's crowding comes from people moving in because islands lack basic services, a problem created by earlier planning.
Called for regional hubs with hospitals, universities and transport links, and for capital-area flats to match demand.

decisions: Three written ministerial answers on the drug prevalence survey were tabled.
Two bills (amending the Audit Act and Law 2013/3) were introduced for first reading.
Preliminary debate on the Constitution amendment bill on asset disclosure was closed with no other speakers.
Debate on the government's re-employment bill was closed after 14 speakers.
The sitting recessed from 10:31 to 11:01 and then resumed with the Fenaka audit resolution.
The constitutional amendment bill from the North Galolhu member was accepted by the House and sent to the Finance Committee.
The government employment bill, tabled by the Guraidhoo member, was accepted and sent to the National Development and Heritage Committee.
The Land Transport Act amendment bill (Law No. 2009/5) was accepted and sent to the National Development and Heritage Committee.
The House recessed from 11:39 to 13:00; committee meetings were scheduled for that morning and afternoon.
The next sitting was set for Wednesday 8 October 2025 at 9:00 am.

votes.what: Accept constitutional amendment bill (North Galolhu member) for study; 93 members, 62 present, 30 needed
Accept government employment bill (Guraidhoo member) for study; 62 present, 31 needed
Accept Land Transport Act amendment bill (North Galolhu member) for study; 62 present, 31 needed
